static.topic: Israel's Knesset elections and proportional representation
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Electoral Systems & Comparative Government
static.whatIsIt: The Knesset is Israel's 120-member unicameral legislature, elected on a nationwide closed-list proportional representation system. A party or bloc needs 61 seats to command a majority, so governments are almost always multi-party coalitions rather than single-party majorities.
static.background: Israel has a history of fragmented coalition politics, with no single party securing a majority in recent cycles. Arab-led parties have historically stayed outside governing coalitions, though Ra'am under Mansour Abbas joined the governing coalition formed in 2021 — the first Arab party to do so — before that arrangement collapsed. The current election has again produced a fragmented house in which Arab-led parties hold 19 seats.
static.geography: Israel, West Asia; the Knesset sits in Jerusalem.
static.socioEconomic: Arab citizens form a significant minority of Israel's population and have historically been under-represented in the executive, making their parties' entry into coalition politics a sensitive domestic issue.
static.whyInNews: Arab-led parties' 19 seats give them potential influence over the next government, while a Jewish former police officer, Yoav Segalovitz, has joined the Islamist party Ra'am and will sit in the new parliament.
static.wayForward: Watch whether cross-community candidacies and Arab-led parties' coalition leverage translate into durable representation, and how the Shin Bet funding inquiry concludes.
prelimsPointers: Knesset has 120 members; 61 seats are needed for a majority.
Israel uses a single nationwide constituency with proportional representation and a minimum vote threshold for entry.
Shin Bet (Shabak) is Israel's internal security agency, distinct from the Mossad, which handles foreign intelligence.
static.mainsAngle: Compare first-past-the-post and proportional representation systems on minority representation and government stability, using Israel's coalition politics as a case study.

static.topic: India–Israel relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & West Asia
static.whatIsIt: India–Israel ties cover defence procurement, agriculture and water technology, cyber and counter-terrorism cooperation, and the I2U2 grouping (India, Israel, UAE, United States) launched in 2022.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but established full diplomatic relations only in 1992. Ties deepened from the late 1990s, with Israel becoming a major defence supplier. India has simultaneously maintained support for a two-state solution and substantive ties with Palestine and Gulf states — a policy often described as de-hyphenation.
static.geography: Israel is located on the eastern Mediterranean, sharing borders with Lebanon, Syria, Jordan and Egypt.
static.socioEconomic: Defence trade, agricultural technology transfer and water management are the main economic pillars of the relationship.
static.whyInNews: Political flux in Israel — an election-integrity inquiry and an unusual cross-community candidacy — affects the stability of a key Indian partner in West Asia.
static.wayForward: India is likely to continue balancing its Israel relationship with its Palestine and Gulf ties, while I2U2 provides a platform for minilateral cooperation.
prelimsPointers: India recognised Israel in 1950; full diplomatic relations were established in 1992.
India supports a two-state solution to the Israel-Palestine question.
I2U2 groups India, Israel, the UAE and the United States.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how India balances its strategic partnership with Israel against its historical ties with Palestine and the Gulf states.

static.topic: Gulf diplomacy and foreign funding of political parties
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance & Political Finance
static.whatIsIt: Gulf states, particularly Qatar, have carved out a role as mediators in regional disputes. Allegations that a foreign state funded a domestic political party raise questions of electoral integrity and external influence.
static.background: Qatar has mediated in several regional conflicts and hosts political offices of various factions, which has made it a recurring subject of external-funding allegations. Israel's Shin Bet launched its inquiry into whether Ra'am received money from Qatar at the request of the elections chief; both Qatar and Ra'am deny the accusation.
static.geography: Gulf region, West Asia.
static.socioEconomic: Foreign funding of political parties is a governance concern globally, with most democracies imposing disclosure or prohibition regimes on foreign donations.
static.whyInNews: The Shin Bet inquiry into alleged Qatari funding of Ra'am is running alongside the certification of Israel's election result.
static.wayForward: Transparent political-finance disclosure rules and clear separation between mediation diplomacy and domestic political funding would reduce such disputes.
prelimsPointers: Shin Bet is Israel's internal security service; Mossad handles foreign intelligence.
Qatar has played a prominent mediation role in West Asian conflicts.
Allegations of foreign funding of political parties are denied by both Qatar and Ra'am in this case.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the risks that foreign funding of political parties poses to electoral sovereignty, and evaluate disclosure-based regulatory responses.

prelims: Knesset: Israel's 120-member legislature; 61 seats needed for a majority, making coalitions essential.
Ra'am is an Arab-led Islamist party in Israel led by Mansour Abbas; Arab-led parties together hold 19 Knesset seats.
Shin Bet is Israel's internal security agency; it opened the inquiry into alleged Qatari funding of Ra'am at the elections chief's request.
Yoav Segalovitz, a Jewish former police officer, has joined Ra'am and will represent it in the newly elected parliament.
stories.mainsQuestion: Proportional representation is often credited with better minority representation but criticised for fragmented and unstable governments. Examine this trade-off with reference to Israel's coalition politics and draw comparative lessons for India.

stories.headline: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ends after 35 years
stories.summary: The 35-year-old United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has ended after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, according to the UN chief. The announcement was made on Sunday, as reported by Reuters and carried by ThePrint. The mission had operated in the disputed Western Sahara region for over three decades. Its termination underscores the Security Council's difficulty in sustaining consensus on peacekeeping mandates. The development is significant for Morocco and the wider North African region, where the Western Sahara dispute remains unresolved.
stories.whyItMatters: Tests understanding of UNSC mandate renewal, veto politics, peacekeeping operations, and UN reform debates—key GS-II international relations themes. Also relevant to India's role as a major troop contributor and its UNSC permanent membership claim.

perspectives.take: Carries a Reuters report framing the development as the end of a 35-year UN mission after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate; focuses on multilateral gridlock rather than assigning blame.

static.topic: United Nations Security Council and Peacekeeping Mandates
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance / United Nations
static.whatIsIt: The UN Security Council authorises and renews peacekeeping mandates; if it does not renew, the mission ends. The UNSC has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms.
static.background: The UN was founded in 1945 and has six principal organs. India is a founding member and one of the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4—India, Brazil, Germany, Japan—campaigns for permanent UNSC expansion, but the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.whyInNews: The 35-year-old UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara ended after the Security Council failed to renew its mandate, the UN chief said.
static.wayForward: Member states could pursue renewed UNSC consultations on the mandate and, more broadly, advance Council reform to reduce veto-driven paralysis in peacekeeping decisions.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for 2-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN HQ is in New York.
India is a founding UN member and a major troop contributor to peacekeeping.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim for permanent UNSC membership rests on representativeness, population and peacekeeping contributions; assess obstacles such as veto politics and the African Ezulwini Consensus.

stories.headline: Binance outflows hit $3.6 billion after $6.3 billion crypto hack
stories.summary: Binance, one of the world's largest crypto exchanges, saw roughly $3.6 billion in net outflows after a hack in which about $6.3 billion in crypto assets was reported to have been moved. The exchange temporarily suspended withdrawals on Thursday to investigate the incident and stabilise its systems, and said the pace of fund movement eased once the initial surge of withdrawals subsided. The episode highlights the concentration and liquidity risk that runs through centralised crypto trading venues, where a single security failure can trigger a self-reinforcing run. For investors, the immediate questions are about asset recovery, custody guarantees and the reliability of exchange-level safeguards rather than about the underlying tokens alone.
stories.whyItMatters: Exchange-level hacks and resulting bank-run dynamics are the clearest illustration of crypto's systemic and consumer-protection risks, feeding directly into India's debate on VDA taxation, PMLA obligations and CBDC design.

perspectives.take: Frames the event through investor impact — heavy outflows, a temporary withdrawal freeze and what the run means for customers and holders; global business-paper lens, no Indian regulatory angle developed.

static.topic: Crypto Assets and Virtual Digital Asset (VDA) Regulation in India
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Financial Sector, Money & Banking, Government Policy
static.whatIsIt: India does not recognise crypto assets as legal tender and has no dedicated statute governing them. Instead, VDAs are regulated indirectly through tax law, anti-money-laundering rules and reporting obligations, while the RBI has pursued a central bank digital currency (e-rupee) as the official digital alternative.
static.background: The RBI's 2018 circular barring banks from dealing with crypto businesses was set aside by the Supreme Court in 2020 (Internet and Mobile Association of India v. RBI). Budget 2022 defined 'virtual digital asset' and introduced a 30% tax on gains plus 1% TDS on transfers. In 2023, VDA businesses were brought within the Prevention of Money Laundering Act framework and required to register with FIU-IND. A draft Bill proposing a ban on private cryptocurrencies was circulated in 2019 but never enacted; a subsequent Bill was listed for Parliament without being introduced.
static.socioEconomic: Retail participation in crypto in India is significant and largely unregulated at the point of sale, raising concerns about household losses, mis-selling and the use of VDAs for fraud and money laundering.
static.whyInNews: A large-scale hack at Binance and the resulting multi-billion-dollar outflow revive questions about the safety of centralised exchanges and the adequacy of India's indirect regulatory approach.
static.wayForward: Move from indirect taxation and AML coverage towards a clear statutory framework that settles classification, licensing, custody and disclosure norms, while advancing the e-rupee pilot and coordinating through multilateral bodies such as the IMF-FSB synthesis framework endorsed under India's 2023 G20 presidency.
prelimsPointers: 30% tax on VDA gains and 1% TDS on transfers were introduced via Budget 2022, effective from the 2022-23 financial year.
The Supreme Court struck down the RBI's 2018 banking ban on crypto dealings in 2020.
VDA businesses were brought under the PMLA in 2023 and must register with FIU-IND.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether India's tax-and-AML-first approach to crypto assets is sufficient to protect retail investors and financial stability, or whether a dedicated regulatory statute is now unavoidable.

static.topic: Financial Stability, Capital Flows and Cyber Risk in Digital Finance
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Financial Stability; Internal Security — Cyber Security
static.whatIsIt: Financial stability refers to the resilience of the financial system against shocks. Digital and crypto markets introduce new transmission channels — concentrated exchange exposure, 24x7 trading, cross-border capital movement and cyber vulnerabilities — that can amplify shocks faster than traditional banking channels.
static.background: Global standard-setters have repeatedly flagged crypto-asset risk to financial stability. The IMF-FSB synthesis paper on crypto-asset policy, endorsed during India's G20 presidency in 2023, called for comprehensive regulation and supervision rather than outright bans, alongside macroprudential safeguards. India's own cyber-security architecture is anchored in CERT-In, the IT Act and NCIIPC for critical infrastructure.
static.socioEconomic: Crypto market stress can spill into household wealth and, where exchanges are used for payments or remittances, into real-economy transactions in emerging economies with weak consumer redress.
static.whyInNews: The Binance hack and the resulting withdrawal surge demonstrate how quickly a single cyber incident can translate into a liquidity event at a systemically important exchange.
static.wayForward: Strengthen exchange-level disclosure and reserve-audit norms, build cross-border supervisory coordination, and treat large crypto intermediaries as critical digital infrastructure subject to cyber-resilience and incident-reporting standards.
prelimsPointers: The IMF-FSB synthesis paper on crypto-asset regulation was endorsed under India's 2023 G20 presidency.
CERT-In is India's national nodal agency for cyber-incident response under the IT Act.
NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure in India.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how cyber vulnerabilities in digital financial intermediaries can become systemic financial stability risks, and suggest safeguards for emerging economies.

prelims: Binance temporarily suspended withdrawals to investigate the hack before resuming operations as outflows eased.
Reported figures: about $6.3 billion in crypto moved in the hack and roughly $3.6 billion in resulting net outflows.
India taxes VDA gains at 30% with 1% TDS on transfers, and VDA businesses are covered under the PMLA and must register with FIU-IND.
The RBI's 2018 ban on bank dealings with crypto businesses was set aside by the Supreme Court in 2020.
stories.mainsQuestion: Large-scale hacks at centralised crypto exchanges can trigger rapid liquidity runs. In this context, critically examine India's current regulatory approach to virtual digital assets and suggest a framework that balances innovation, investor protection and financial stability.

onThisDay.title: Balfour Declaration
onThisDay.description: British Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour issued a declaration supporting the establishment of a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, while stating that the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities would not be prejudiced. It became a key document in the creation of Israel and the modern Middle East conflict.
